Prevention: Use certified seed or disease-free sets.
Any material suspected to be infected should not be planted
Avoid overcrowded crops, damp conditions and sheltered or shaded sites.
Ensure that plant spacing is at 30cm x 10cm
Maintain good weed control to ensure airflow through the crop
Avoid overhead irrigation method to keep the follage dry.
Do not apply water to leaves.
Use hose pipes which deliver water straight to the soil
It is important not to leave bulbs in the soil year after year as the fungus can remain dormant and infect new crops when conditions are wet and humid
Practice crop rotation, have a break of three years.
Rotate with non host crops like maize or sweet potatoes
Monitoring: The disease is characterised by pale green/ yellowish/brownish areas of irregular size and shape (oval or cylindrical) on affected leaves or seed stalks.
These areas may consist of yellow and green layers of tissue (mottles)
Leaves become girdled (ring backed) in the region where mildew develops and they eventually collapse.
The dead leaf tissue is rapidly colonised by purple blotch, which is dark in colour and obscures downy mildew
Dead leaf tips can be seen within defined (localised) spots in a field
Take action as soon as symptoms of the disease are seen
This disease can damage mature bulbs which should be checked at harvest.
If the bulbs have any symptoms or spongy necks they should be discarded and destroyed
Direct Control: Rogue out infected plants as soon as symptoms are seen, burn them or bury deepy.

Restrictions: Use personal protective equipment when handling and applying pesticides, follow the label recommendations.
Do not eat, drink, smoke when mixing or applying pesticides
Mancozeb at the rate of 20g per 10 litres of water every two weeks from first sign of disease.
Bravo 720SC to prevent development of resistance
U (Unlikely to prevent acute hazard in normal use).
Chlorothalonil 720g/l (Bravo 720SC) at the rate of 20g per 10 litres of water as soon as you see the disease and repeat every two weeks.
